title: The Last Tinker™: City of Colors
text: Repetitive, tedious and frustrating. Okay, this is not a *horrible* game, but it ain't too great either. The most positive things I can think of are good graphics and it seems to have a decent storyline (I guess). But the camera views are difficult and frustrating. The part of the game I am currently on features very bland, repetitive, boring combat. You have to run half a mile (slight exaggeration) away from an enemy, then quickly turn around to face him and then shoot beams at him. Problem is, by the time you've turned around and aimed at him you only have two seconds to fire beams at him before you have to run away again. Those beams are your ONLY way of fighting the enemy and you have to hit him a whole bunch of times, so these battles are lengthy and tedious. Mind you, there were earlier parts of the game that had better combat in which you punch and physically hit enemies, and this might just be a phase I'm on now. But why include this phase at all? And will this phase return later on? The poor camera controls add to the tedious and frustrating nature of the game. One final flaw I'd like to mention is that the whole game seems just a little laggy and jumpy. I'm using Intel HD Integrated graphics (no dedicated graphics card), but Mass Effect 2 runs perfectly on my computer and this game runs... sluggishly. It's as if the camera cannot keep up with the action and some frames are skipped. I have enjoyed parts of this game but there are flaws which cannot allow me to recommend it.

title: The Last Tinker™: City of Colors
text: TL;DR : Description gives wrong expectations, but the game is still fun. This is more an adventure game than a platformer. Many people complain that this is not a difficult/challenging platformer. But it's not meant to be. It's a kid-friendly, easy platformer. So of course most of the platforming and combat is easy, and a lot of things are automated. The problem comes from the "inspired by" part of the description. This proves once again it's rarely a good idea to say your game is inspired by this or that because people will expect a very similar game and be disappointed. The game may be wrongly advertised, but that doesn't mean the game is bad. You just have to expect a fun and colorful, kid-friendly (both in terms of content and difficulty) adventure game with platforming elements. Not an actual platformer like the two games this one is said to be inspired by.

title: The Last Tinker™: City of Colors
text: First impressions are very important when it comes to making a game, and when it comes to this one, it isn't hard to see why a lot of people dismiss it as a "meh" game: Combat is rather simplistic, the story clearly is about the evils of racism and how it ruins communites, and infamously about how it feels nothing like what it claims to be paying homage to. But then you play a little more, and you see that the game touches down on more than just racism during your 5-7 hour adventure. It will delve into the dangers of excessive paranoia and fear of the unknown, tell the story of a man who wastes his life away at the bar instead of trying to solve all his problems like a man, and of course that there is nothing wrong with helping someone that you normally aren't really friends with.. In dark times, even the bullies that pester you need your help, and in turn can become a close friend. Combat, while it still is button mashy, at least gets a bit more interesting as you progress through the game, getting new powers that allow you to switch it up a bit, such as the power to stun a large enemy so you can deal a critical blow from behind, or even cause them to suddenly start running in fear off of a cliff or into spiked bushes of death. Late in the game there is even some enemies that require you to vary your attacks in order to beat it, so you can't just button mash your whole way, as well as the fact that sometimes you need to use a later-earned ranged attack to deal with other threats, giving you something different besides jush mashing the left mouse button. However, the game most certainly is no Banjo & Kazooie or Jak and Daxter, what with the collection element of the game being completely optional and only used for small bonus content, nothing really big (unless you like lookin at concept art), and the platforming being mostly simplified (I say mostly, because there still is a few segments that require your input, such as jumping during rail grinds and the general timing of platforming). Rather, this is more of a 3D semi-platformer bawler of sorts, and for the kids, I think it is a fairly decent little game. Not only does it leave you to ponder a few things afterwards about the content it tackles, but it also is a fun title full of life and personality, and a few chuckles here and there.. For the hardcore sort, however, maybe you might wanna look elsewhere, because while there is some challenge in this game, I don't think it'll be enough to keep more serious gamers engaged for long, as indicated again by the negative reputation this game sadly has.

title: The Last Tinker™: City of Colors
text: The creators of The Last Tinker attempted to create a 3D-platformer like they were in the good old days about ten or fifteen years ago. The intentions are good, but unfortunately the creators must have thought the development of this genre during the last few years was a massive improvement. There certainly were improvements like ditching the classic live system or autosaving. But for me, on-rails-platforming is not an improvement. On-rails-platforming means that the protagonist, Koru in the case of The Last Tinker, jumps automatically. You just walk around while holding a button and overcome the obstacles automatically. Some games like the AC series have an excuse for such a simplification: a lot of background stuff is going on which you have to keep track off, focussing on precise jumping all the time would be too hard. However, this excuse is not valid for The Last Tinker. Even though he refers to something slightly different, I would like to quote Ben Croshaw here: "[...] there's no challenge to this! This is not platforming, this is just walking down a very unusually-shaped corridor."  Fortunately the developers of The Last Tinker made this observation as well and included timing sections to add some challenge to the platforming. (For the record, the same holds for the developers of Enslaved.) Enough about the "platforming", let us look at other aspects of the game. It is rich in variety after all.  There is some combat, of course, the common button-smashing combo-based combat. There are some railsliding sections, where you have to continuously switch between rails to not smash into obstacles. And there are many puzzles of various types which are usually nice, but not diffifcult. What I really like about The Last Tinker is that it tells its story not exclusively by the means of cutscenes and dialogues, but also by the environment itself. You can literally see how the city is estranged and united again. Conclusion: The Last Tinker has its weaknesses, but it shines in other aspects. It is not challenging, but also doesn't get boring easily. Overall The Last Tinker offers a very nice experience.

title: The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel
text: The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel I picked this game (and some other ones) up on a whim just to satisfy a JRPG craving I was having and was really surprised by game itself. However, before I go on with giving a decent recommendation let me first preface and say most of the negative things you hear about this game are true. The game really develops at a slow pace, this is undeniable however if you consider this is the first in a four game series it is understandable. The voice acting is generally terrible, and there is no option to my knowledge to switch to Japanese language with English subtitles. Lastly the game doesn’t do anything incredibly unique in terms of mechanics making it rather unsurprising in terms of game play. That out of the way I was never once bothered by the lack of originality of game play mechanics, what is offered is what I expected and I didn’t feel that it detracted from the overall game. The story is unique, the characters are compelling, and the world feels sufficiently fleshed out to where I never felt like a dissonant element was introduced that broke my experience. In fact I was so absorbed in the world the developers created I played the game three more times just to ensure I got to see everything that is offered. The DLC’s offered are completely optional and are primarily just cosmetics minus some low priced game play boosts such as money, crafting material and some accessories. Most of which can be achieved through normal game play or multiple playthroughs. Anyway, I highly recommend Trails of Cold Steel to anyone that wants to play a solid JRPG and can handle bad voice acting.

title: The Legend of Heroes: Trails of Cold Steel
text: I'm a big fan of Trails in the sky series, and Falcom always make games that are enjoyable. Trails of Cold Steel is nonetheless extent of Falcom's successful story-rich series; in terms of world-building, there really is nothing like this series. World goes around without you; it does progress with you, but every npc has little stories and problems that they're dealing with, and it's up to you to talk to them. NPCs always have something to say about the things that happened in their town, and if you like walking around the town talking to people about some weird stuffs that you don't even have to really know, then you will spend more time reading texts than playing and progressing main storyline. Characters will look as cliched as it can be, but as story progresses, you will start to see more of them, so it adds kind of weird depth to their personality. Combat system is tight; if you don't let your guard down and stun enemies before you engage, game won't be a challenge even on hard mode, but it will still keep you at the edge of your seat, and focused because link system is all about that quick button pushing. Soundtrack is still good, just like all the previous series. All in all, I must say I'm satisfied with my purchase, I simply couldn't resist the urges of playing more trails games because I fell in love with this world that Falcom built.

text: I didn't expect to be as captivated by this as I ended up being. text: The monster inside is a short visual novel in a Nuit Noir style. The story is somewhat typical for noir styled movies / books - being an old detective who quit being a cop before gets into a strange story. The gameplay consists only of reading and pressing few elements you find in the game specifically designed for progressing further. There is no combat in this game, nor is there is any challenge, besides if you consider reading a challenge. The graphic is simple but with some fitting details (like night butterflies around a lamp, smoke from a cigarette). Since it is black and white, there is not much detail to the areas but it works especially in combination with some of the text provided. The progress consists only of pressing next and finding some clues on the investigation sites. The music was great for this short novel, making it easier to immerse into the noir style of the game. Since it takes only around 20-30 minutes to complete the game and its free, just try it out. I hope this review helps you making the decision if its worth buying this game. title: The Monster Inside
text: ...is a film-noir text-based story. Jack, a private investigator with a dark past, is approached by a woman that sets him on a case to investigate a series of murders. There is little to say, as this isn't really a game at all, more like a short story or chronical. Your character is the narrator, and you progress through a few dialog choices, going from a short scene to another. As you read the story, you have a simple and lightly-animated image of the location. One word to describe your experience is atmospheric. While simple, the monochrome images are accompanied by gorgeous music that puts you in the right mood. I suppose achievement hunters can probably see this as an easy opportunity to make a few points. You can't make mistakes or make a wrong move, nothing will challenge you intellectually or morally. It's linear, has no branching path, and by Chapter 5 it's all very predictable. There won't be any reason to give this a second playthrough, unless you just want to listen to the music playing while reading an actual book. Probably my shortest review. On paper, wouldn't be more than a one-page column in a collection of short stories. However, it's free and won't take much of your time. Go ahead, take 15-20 minutes and give it a try. If you didn't like your experience, you didn't waste much. —————————————————————————

title: The Monster Inside
text: Another supernaturally-themed detective thriller. Given that my last review was for Adam Wolfe, I wouldn't blame you for thinking I'm on some sort of binge here...but it's all just coincidence yer honour, I swear. And while this is definitely the inferior of the two, it's also the more inexpensive of the two (i.e. free!), so I'm gonna go easy on it. But only this one time. Capeesh? There's three main things people tend to expect from "visual novels". The first is a nice visual style, and this game most certainly has that (with nice sound design and dandy music, to boot). The second is a good story, and while there's the hint of something potentially noteworthy here, it's all too brief and half-baked to carry much weight (the narrative feels like it wraps up just as it starts to get going). Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly if one were to classify this as a "game", there's the issue of player agency...of which there is extraordinarily little in this title. I even re-played the first half to see if different "choices" had much bearing on proceedings: they didn't. Just seven linear chapters and one ending, unless I'm mistaken; a theory which seems borne out by the fact that you can get 100% Achievements just by playing the game through once (so there is THAT, if you're the Achievement-hunting type). As a brief and only mildly interactive "experience", it's alright. A long way from amazing, but perfectly alright. Especially for free. No, scrap that: ONLY for free. I'd be hesitant to recommend this for even zero dollars and ninety-nine cents, the minimum RRP of any game asking money on Steam. It's much closer to an impressive proof-of-concept than anything truly tangible or greatly worthy of your time. (Curiously enough, I see that the same devs were responsible for another game on Steam called TIMEframe. If you're looking for a similarly short yet somehow much "deeper" experience than this - and are willing to part with at least a little dough in order to achieve such ends - you'd be better served looking that-a-way. It packs a much, much bigger punch than this one does.) That said, and I'll say it again...this IS free. So while there's not a whole hell of a lot to recommend, there also ain't a whole hell of a lot to be hating on. There's definitely worse ways to waste fifteen minutes of your time, should you find yourself at a bit of a loose end. Verdict: 6.5/10.
